text: Meanwhile, the Cyclops had a different life in a different poem. Hesiod, writing around 700 BC, names three Cyclopes: Bron-teez, Stair-oh-peez, and Ar-geez. Thunder, Lightning, and Bright. They forge the thunderbolt for Zeus. And Hesiod is the one who says it plainly: 'one eye only was set in the midst of their foreheads.' These are not cannibal shepherds. They are craftsmen, working for the king of the gods. Same name, same eye, completely different job. The scholar Walter Boor-kert suggested the smith Cyclopes may reflect real guilds of metalworkers. Later poets merged the two. Virgil puts Bron-teez and Stair-oh-peez in a forge under Etna. By the fifth century BC, the Cyclopes are living on Sicily. Euripides sets a comic satyr play about Pollifeemus beside Mount Etna. The historian Thoo-sididdeez lists the Cyclopes among Sicily's earliest inhabitants, then adds that he cannot say what race they were, or where they came from. He also reports that locals believed the smith-god had a forge in the Aeolian islands, judging by the flame at night and the smoke by day. By the third century BC, Thee-ockritus has Pollifeemus singing love songs to a sea nymph, and worrying about his one long eyebrow. Even cannibals get a love life.
